sections.text: Lord Shri Krishna continued: This phenomenal creation, which is both ephemeral and eternal, is like a tree, but having its seed above in the Highest and its ramifications on this earth below. The scriptures are its leaves, and he who understands this, knows.

Its branches shoot upwards and downwards, deriving their nourishment from the Qualities; its buds are the objects of sense; and its roots, which follow the Law causing mans regeneration and degeneration, pierce downwards into the soil.

In this world its true form is not known, neither its origin nor its end, and its strength is not understood, until the tree with its roots striking deep into the earth is hewn down by the sharp axe of non-attachment.

We have completed chapter 14, Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga. And now we will be starting discussion of Chapter 15, Purushottam Yoga -- Yoga of the Supreme Purusha. In Chapter 13 we have seen the difference between the field and its knower.
The Prakriti is the field, and the one which is aware of the field is the knower of the field. So at my individual level, we have learned that this body is the field. The one who is aware of the body is the knower of the field.
So the body is part of the Prakriti. But I, the knower is part of the Purusha, the manifestation of Purusha in me. This Purusha which is imperishable, right now I consider it to be perishable because it is identified with this perishable body.
To make this connection between the Purusha and Prakriti at both my individual level and at the universal level, we learned in chapter 14 that the Purusha is the father of all the beings and Prakriti is the womb of all the beings in this world. So Prakriti is the mother and Purusha is the father. Any being which is born at any place, to any womb -- Bhagavan said, consider this great Prakriti as the womb and I am the seed-giving Father.
We see the variety of beings and things in this world; that variety is explained by these three Gunas, the three binding ropes which bind this imperishable Purusha to this perishable manifestation. This variety of things and beings are created by the permutation and combination of these Gunas, the three modes of material nature. This variety of things and beings around me create my Sansaar.
My relationship with these things and beings is my Sansaar. This Sansaar is ever changing Samsaratiyeti Sansaar. That which is constantly changing is Sansaar.
Sansaar does not remain same. That which was there a minute ago has already changed. It has already passed.
So we constantly are struggling with this ever changing Sansaar. This Sansaar continues to grow. When I was just a single person and a student, my Sansaar was limited to me and my parents.
Then you get married -- so now you have become two. Your problem plus her problem, and then we have children. So not only my problem, her problem, but also his problem.
A few years ago when I used to go to India, I used to have only three houses to visit -- my three brothers. Now when I go there, it is not only my brothers houses but their children -- they are married, their in-laws. So by the time Im done, the 15 days are just gone, just meeting with all their relatives.
Because my Sansaar has grown. Bhajagovindam says: Bala tat krida sakthah, taruna tat taruni sakthah, vruddha tavat chinta sakthah. When I was a child, I was engaged in plays and toys. When I was a young man, I was engaged in chasing girls.
When I became an old man, Im just overwhelmed by worries. I said well why would that be? You should be relieved. So I was actually looking forward to an old age.
Because I thought the old age means my children will be married. I will have no worries then I will be completely free. Now that I have become an old man, I realize how true that verse was.
Not only did I have to worry about myself, my family, my children, but also their children. So my Sansaar has grown so large. To detach from the Sansaar is increasingly becoming more and more difficult as the Sansaar grows.
So this chapter opens up with the allegory of this Sansaar. It says: Urdhvamulah adhah shakham ashvattham prahuhu avyayam, Chandamsi Yasya Parnani, Yastam Veda sa Veda vit -- describing this Sansaar by using this allegory where it is like an upside-down tree. Now this allegory has been used in the Upanishads.
In the Katha Upanishad, in the sixth portion, the Lord of death Yama indicates to Nachiketa that this Sansaar is like the upside-down tree. The roots are in heaven and it is spreading in this world below. So my Sansaar right now is like that Urdhvamuna.
Its source is up above. We always say anything which is higher say up Bhagavan kaha Upar. So this world as we see Bhagavad Gita and the Upanishad say the source is Apa.
Source is somewhere beyond my perception. Urdhvamuna adas Sakaha all the branches are below. That which I see growing is here in my world.
I see its effect, I dont see the cause. So in our normal tree, roots are not perceivable. They are not perceived.
They are below under the ground. But we see the trunk and we see the branches. And these branches continue to grow.
And this Sansaar is like that. As we have learned a few lectures ago, the return in farming is thousand fold. So traditionally the farmers were the richest people.
Even the kings were farmers. Janakaraja found Sita while tilling the land, because farming was the most profitable business, most rewarding business. You sow one seed and a thousand come out.
So the growth is exponential in anything in nature. The tree grows exponentially. My Sansaar is like that -- it grows exponentially beyond my control.
I do one action and it creates a thousand reactions. The allegory of the tree shows this: one action generates a thousand connections in my Sansaar. And its source is Apaba Urdhvamulaha Adasakaha.
I see the branches of my Sansaar here below. Prahuhu Abyam the wise people talk about this tree of Sansaar is something which has the roots above the branches below Chandansi, Yasya, Panani. The Vedas are its leaves.
This verse about the Vedas being the leaves needs explanation because the connection is not immediately obvious. We have seen the commentaries by various scholars. Bhagavan Sankaracharya says the tree is explained as Ashvattha.
Because when you break down the word Ashvattha, it becomes that which does not remain the same tomorrow. Therefore this tree of Sansaar is explained as Asvathaha. And therefore that which promotes growth to this tree is the Vedas. The knowledge of Vedas, the instructions in Vedas, when followed by a person, his Sansaar grows healthily.
By knowing this Sansaar and Prakriti, I more and more grow my Sansaar here. So these Vedas, the knowledge grows this tree of Sansaar in my life, in yours, in his Chandansi, Yasya, Pranani, Yastam, Vedasa, Veda Vid. And he who knows, he is a Veda knower.
One who knows both the roots and the branches of this tree, he knows the entire tree. So when I look at the tree I already know because I am a Veda knower of the trees that the roots are below in the ground. So There is a knowledge about where the roots are for the tree that makes my knowledge of the tree complete.
So right now my knowledge of my Sansaar is incomplete. Because I only know what I see. So I only believe that what I see is the reality beyond my perception.
I dont see there is reality. The other day we are explaining myth to Meda and say myth is something, a made up story to explain something. And she said okay then my English homework is a myth because its made of stories in it.
So we consider that seeing is believing. Everything I see as real is real. Everything else is myth.
And therefore our knowledge is incomplete about this tree of Sansaar. I will know this tree of Sansaar completely when I know the roots, what the source of this tree of Sansaar is. Thats why we are lacking for one side.
So therefore I say one who knows this, he knows the Vedas. Vedas explain both the cause and effect. The roots and its tree.
So one who knows both is the Veda knower. Not the one who is only rooted in the Prakriti or this world. Only Yastam Vedasa Vedavid.
Such a person knows the Vedas. Adhacha Urdhvam Prasuta Tashishaka, Guna Pravruddha, Vishe Pravalaha. So our Sansaar is now described using this allegory of a tree.
So that we understand how my world works. We talked about Prakriti in detail in last chapter but we have still stopped at. But these are the Gunas which are binding me and I need to go beyond these Gunas.
Now we are learning about this Sansaar which is constantly changing. And how can I liberate myself from this Sansaar root? The cause for this is the Purusha. Unless there is consciousness, there is no Sansaar.
How this Sansaar is rooted in this consciousness is what Im trying to understand. That this tree grows in my world. Adha Cha Urdham, Prasuta Tashya Shah.
Its branches are up and also below my world of ideas. Prakriti in the lower world where I live in. But I also have ideas about the higher nature. So my ideas go both ways.
They go up and they go down. I think about mundane thing but I also think about the sacred things. So my branches of my Sansaar is spreading in both directions in my Prakriti in my day to day life.
But also what is beyond my day to day life. Guna Pravrudha, Vishaya pravalaha. These branches are nourished by the Gunas. They get more and more entangled into this prakruti.
Bound by these Gunas I get more and more entangled in my world here because of the Gunas, my vasanas, my tendencies bind me to this world. My tendency is the music. So I somehow will always have to have some kind of a musical event because my Gunas is binding me.
So these Gunas are binding me into this world below. Guna pravruddha, vishaya pravalaha and the sense objects are the buds. So the sense objects have the potential to grow my Sansaar. If I see something which is of my liking, then my Sansaar will grow in that direction.
As we have seen, given opportunity, I have these latent tendencies. And when the right environment is given to me, those tendencies will play out -- first as desires and then as actions. So if I dont have a chance, if there is no field then those tendencies will remain dormant.
So I may be the nicest person if there is no opportunity given to me to get bribed. I have never taken a bribe in my life, but I may have a tendency to take a bribe which was never given an opportunity. The sense objects are buds.
This opportunity presenting itself will then grow that tendency in me as desire and into actions. So the sense objects are the buds which have the capability to grow my Sansaar in the direction of my tendencies, depending on whether Im sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic. The sense objects will grow my Sansaar in that direction.
Adaachar mulani anusanthatani and while I am functioning in this world bound by these Gunas, I am also developing my roots in this prakrit in this world. When we first moved to Richmond, because we moved from Northern Virginia, we were pretty active there. You know, we were running all these classes and all my friends, they say, Rajan, its not too far, only two hours.
So anytime we have an event, you come down to Northern Virginia. So first about few months we did that, you know, they will have a music party and they will call me and we go down there, we will have music party, we call them and they come down here. Gradually we started having roots here in Richmond.
You know, we have friends here, our own group, and we have classes. So now that we have grown our roots here in Richmond, we gradually get detached from those Northern Virginia friends. Now they call me and I say, yeah, but I dont have time -- I have activities here, I have classes here, so I cant come.

The Ashvattha tree described in these verses presents a powerful mirror for self-examination. Notice how the word Ashvattha itself means that which does not remain the same tomorrow - reminding us that our entire world of relationships, possessions, and circumstances is in constant flux. Yet we keep planting our roots deeper into this ever-changing soil, establishing ourselves in jobs, cities, and social circles as if they were permanent. Consider today: where have you been growing roots that bind you more tightly to the impermanent? The verse tells us that the Vedas - knowledge itself - are the leaves that nourish this tree. Even our learning can become an attachment that expands rather than liberates us.
The remedy offered is remarkably specific: asanga-shastrena dridhena - with the strong weapon of non-attachment, cut this tree. This is not about abandoning responsibilities, but about loosening the grip of identification. Try this practice: at the end of each day, identify one thing you clung to - an opinion, an outcome, a preference - and consciously release it. Ask yourself: What would remain of me if this were taken away? The one who truly knows this tree, says Krishna, is the knower of the Vedas. True wisdom is not just understanding your world, but understanding its source and your relationship to that source.
